For example, a heat pump with COP 3 on a grid with 0.8 kg CO2e/kWh electricity will emit 0.267 kg CO2e per kWh heat, while a 90% efficient gas boiler emits 0.203 kg CO2e per kWh heat (using 0.183 kg CO2e/kWh gas).

**Heat pumps cost more upfront but save over time—in 2026, a typical installed heat pump runs $5,500-$12,000, while a gas boiler costs $4,000-$8,000, yet after IRA rebates, many households pay less for the heat pump.** The lifetime cost comparison, covering 15 years with maintenance and energy, often favors the heat pump, especially with incentives.
At these rates, a heat pump with an HSPF2 of 9.5 costs about $0.12 per 100,000 BTU of heat, while a gas boiler at 95% AFUE costs $0.16 per 100,000 BTU—making heat pumps cheaper.

Lifecycle emissions (manufacturing, installation, disposal of equipment) are not included: heat pumps typically have higher upfront lifecycle emissions than gas boilers, but these are offset by lower operational emissions within 5-10 years of use.
Lifecycle emissions use average values for mid-efficiency systems over a 15-year lifespan: 150 kg CO2e/year for gas boilers, 300 kg CO2e/year for heat pumps.
